title: Theory, Instruments, Scales and Modelling
author: Chris Wheadon
summary: Wheadon, who teaches psychometrics on an Oxford assessment masters, argues that every piece of measurement should be interrogated through four questions: what is the theory, the instruments, the scales and the modelling. He makes theory the starting point because it disciplines inference and keeps assessors from vague constructs like general ability or from absurd correlations such as table-tapping speed. Using No More Marking's writing assessment as a case, he explains how instruments should be as transparent as possible to the theory, trading off authenticity against narrowness. He explains why scales in assessment are harder than physical scales, with writing age as a deliberately value-laden choice, and why modelling comes last. The post is short but gives a clear conceptual framework for assessment validity.
points: Start with a credible theory of what you are measuring, otherwise you risk tests that merely correlate with success, such as table-tapping speed.
Instruments should be as transparent as possible to the theory; replicating real tasks imports irrelevant domains, while narrowing too far loses contact with reality.
Educational scales are harder to fix than physical ones, so writing age depends on a theoretical position about the continuity of writing development.
Modelling is last and serves efficiency and sharper inference, such as reducing teacher judging time, not defining the construct.
The memorable teaching device is a daily quiz question forcing students to ask what theory, instruments and scales sit under any model.
quotes: Starting with theory ensures that you are careful with your inferences, leads you to avoid terms such as intelligence, creativity, merit or general ability that plagued psychometrics in the past.

There may well be some plausible connection between psychophysics and ability to succeed in later education, but you need to start with the theory not the test or risk a school filled with furiously tapping pupils unable to perform algebraic manipulations!

The key is to choose assessment instruments as transparent as possible to your underlying theory. This is not easy: simply asking students to replicate a real-world task will mean assessing extraneous and irrelevant domains. But if you narrow the task down too much it loses touch with reality.
With physical properties scales are fixed and meaningful. Weights and measures can be added and subtracted, distances multiplied and trajectories plotted to distant planets we have not yet visited.

Can you ever really compare the writing of a five year old with the writing of an eleven year old? Well, it would seem it would depend on our theory. If both are attempts to convey meaning through the written word, then yes, we can.

Psychometricians aim to fit models to data that increase the efficiency of our assessments and sharpen the inferences we can make. At No More Marking we use statistical models to reduce the time taken for teachers to judge and to enhance insights into the development of writing.
